subtopic: SHACKLING OF CANADIANS IN GERMAN CAMPS

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: SHACKLING OF CANADIANS IN GERMAN CAMPS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a statement concerning the shackling of prisoners of war in German camps. The ' statement appeared in the press this morning.
It should, I think, also be of record in Hansard.
The following information concerning the shackling of prisoners of war in German camps has been made public by agreement between the governments of Canada and the United Kingdom.
Prisoners of the United Kingdom and Canadian forces are still shackled at stalag VIIIB and at other camps.
On February 11 a communication was made to the Swiss government with the request that the views of the governments of the United Kingdom and of Canada on the question of shackling set out therein should be conveyed to the German government. The reply of the German government has recently been communicated through the same channel

Prisoners of War
and it is now possible to make a public statement showing the present position of this distressing matter.
The Geneva convention lays down generally that prisoners of war must be humanely treated and the point at issue between the United Kingdom and Canadian governments and the German government is what constitutes such treatment. The Geneva convention does not attempt to define humane . treatment and lays down no rule about the shackling or binding of prisoners during operations. *
The German government assert that they will renounce measures taken against our prisoners only on the receipt of an assurance that instructions have been issued to our forces forbidding binding of German prisoners in any circumstances whatsoever. We informed the Swiss government in our communication of February 11, and they in turn informed the German government, that instructions had been issued to our armed forces to ensure that all ranks should be acquainted with and observe the terms of the Geneva convention, and that in those instructions it had been made clear that a general order to bind prisoners is illegal and that the issue of any such order is strictly forbidden. The instructions, however, went on to say that circumstances may arise in which binding of prisoners may be necessary and may indeed be in the best interest of the prisoner himself. It is the duty of a prisoner during operations to try to escape and to impede his captors, who must, of course, prevent such action. In such circumstances binding, which must be carried out in a humane manner, is permissible, always provided it is discontinued as soon as immediate operational necessity allows. These views were duly communicated by the Swiss Minister for Foreign Affairs to the German government which has now replied stating that the principle of shackling is made illusory by the above reservation of circumstances, and they, therefore, insist on compliance with their earlier demands.
The Canadian government have scrupulously observed, and will continue scrupulously to observe, not only the terms but also the spirit of the Geneva convention, article 2 of which lays down that prisoners of war shall "at all times be humanely treated and protected". It may be added that the article of the convention, of which Germany was a signatory, also provides that "measures of reprisal against them are forbidden".
It will be recalled that on December 7th last the Swiss government suggested both to the German government and to the governments of the United Kingdom and Canada that "without prejudice to ' the matter in dispute" and in order to "terminate a state of things manifestly contrary to the principles of humanity" all prisoners in their hands should be freed from .their shackles at an agreed hour on December 15. As evidence of their desire to respond fully and promptly to the spirit of the Swiss proposal, the governments of Canada and the United Kingdom gave orders that the German prisoners in their hands who had been shackled should be freed from their bonds on December 12. The German government continued, however, to shackle our men.
The Canadian government in consultation with the government of the United Kingdom is considering what reply should be returned, for the information of the German government, to the Swiss Minister for Foreign Affairs whose skilful and patient handling of this matter is highly appreciated.
The Canadian and United Kingdom governments will, of course, continue to press for the abandonment by the German government of the shackling now in effect.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: CLOSING OF OVERHAUL PLANT OF CANADIAN PACIFIC AIR LINES-REST PERIOD
speechtext: I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Munitions and Supply. I am in receipt of a telegram from the business agent of Aircraft lodge,, international association of . machinists, Vancouver, informing me that R. P. Bell, director general of aircraft production, had ordered the overhaul plant of the Canadian Pacific Air Lines at New Westminster to close because of a dispute over rest periods in the plant. Has the minister been informed of this situation, and has he a statement to make?

speakeroldname: Hon. C. D. HOWE (Minister of Munitions and Supply):
subtopic: CLOSING OF OVERHAUL PLANT OF CANADIAN PACIFIC AIR LINES-REST PERIOD
speechtext:
I believe it was the day before yesterday my department received advice that the employees of the Boeing plant at Vancouver were insisting on a fifteen-minute rest period in each shift. The men gave as their reason the fact that the Canadian Pacific Air Lines overhaul plant at New Westminster were giving a ten-minute rest period in each shift. Those shifts are eight hours long. It has never been the policy in any part of Canada to allow a rest period in an eight-hour shift. As soon as we were advised of the situation at New Westminster we wired out to have the practice stopped. The reply to that on the part of the men was to stage a fifteenr-minute sit-down. As a result, I instructed Mr. Bell to close the plant until we can have an understanding that we can have eight hours work for eight hours' pay. That is the, policy of the department, and it will be applied wherever the eight-hour shift is the practice.

Oil Production

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I would not call it a probationary period. I might mention a specific case. The Minister of Finance has been, as hon. members know, engaged morning, noon and night in connection with financial measures that have come before the house. He would I think have found it impossible to do what he has done in the time he has if he had not had the assistance of an hon. member of the house who it is anticipated will be appointed his parliamentary assistant. I feel that hon. members would regard it as wholly appropriate that assistance which has been most valuable to the government and to the house would not be permitted to pass unrecognized simply for the reason that we have not been able to get the item in the estimates before the house until this stage of the session. Any request that the government may make to recognize services thus far performed will of course be based upon substantial services to the government and to the House of Commons and to the country. I do not think the amount will be large.
I assume the substantial services would have to be proved at the time the supplemental estimates are brought down?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: That is right.

Do I understand that the appointments begin from April I, the beginning of the present fiscal year, and this appropriation is to pay the salaries of those concerned from April 1, 1943 to March 31, 1944?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The appointments will be from the date at which His Excellency the Governor General approves the order in council recommending the appointments. That may be in the course of another day or two. The appointments will not be made until after this bill has received the royal assent. I have just intimated that there have been, I cannot say many but I think two or

three, hon. members of this house who will be appointed as assistants to ministers, including the Minister of Finance and the Minister of National Defence, who have been assisting ministers continuously for some weeks past, in fact for a couple of months. I do not think it would have been possible for the ministers to make the progress they have made with their work without that assistance. The government may ask that such contribution as has been made to the ministry in that period of time be recognized later in a supplementary estimate.

I have always believed that the Minister of Finance has had perhaps the ablest assistants in his department of any minister of finance. We were told that the}-were exceptionally brilliant and capable, and I myself have marvelled at their industry and capacity. Am I to understand that the Minister of Finance had a member of this house helping him because all these brilliant financial men in his department were not able to assist him in doing the work he has done? I do not like to think that the civil servants in the minister's department are as incapable as that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The hon. member for
St. Antoine-Westmount has been assisting me fairly steadily since the first of February. He hoped to be able to relieve me in the house, but of course had no status which would enable him to do so.
He is a member of the house.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: But it would not be appropriate for a private member to answer questions on behalf of the government until he had some authority to do so. So far as that hon. member is concerned he has raised no question about remuneration.
Because he has not been appointed.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
He has not been appointed, but he will be, without any question, and he has been working. He is away to-day. In his absence I hesitate to say anything which he might prefer that I did not say, but my own idea of proper treatment in regard to remuneration was that his remuneration should begin from April 1, which vcould mean that for two months, that is February and March, he would have given his extra services without remuneration. That was my own idea and I know it would be perfectly satisfactory to him. Whether that is being fair to him I do not know; perhaps it is not. But I am sure he has no idea of trying to make this a remunerative thing in any way. The point as far as

he is concerned is a very narrow one, that is, whether his remuneration should begin from the date of the order in council appointing him, or from the first day of this month. I think it should begin from the first day of the fiscal year. I do not know what arrangements other ministers will make with their parliamentary assistants, but that is what I propose for the hon. member for St. Antoine-Westmount.
The hon. member for Davenport said that civil servants in the Department of Finance, to whom he pays deserved tribute, could do everything that a parliamentary assistant could do. But I can assure hon. members that they cannot. There are a great many duties which civil servants, by virtue of the fact that they are civil servants, cannot perform. The assistance I have received during the last two or three months has been necessary to enable me to carry on the work. I am very much pleased that I have been able to avail myself of it, and very happy that I shall have it in the future.

I should like to ask a question, and I might preface it by the old proverb-fools rush in where angels fear to tread. I happen to know who is going to be the minister's assistant, and in my opinion he is capable of being in any cabinet that Canada ever had. But what I want to know is-and it gives me a chance to get this in; some hon. members apparently fear to bring it up- whether this $4,000 is to be subject to income tax. As I understand it, an hon. member cannot get any exemption from income tax on account of his expenses at Ottawa, air mail and telegrams, and that sort of thing. I know this is not a popular subject; it would appear that some hon. members think they might not be reelected if it were mentioned that a member got some exemption for his excessive costs. My own opinion is that any hon. member who fears for his reelection because he tells the truth should not be in this House of Commons. I do not have to worry that the people in my riding will not back me because I tell the truth. It has been said by the Prime Minister, and I do not know of any better authority we could get, that he hoped, and rightly so, that the. parliament of Canada would be made up of representatives of labour, of agriculture, and if I remember his words correctly, particularly of soldiers who are doing everything for us to-day. I ask hon. members of this house how a soldier serving for $1.30 or $1.50 a day can save enough money so that when he comes back he will be able to run for parliament and possibly be appointed an assistant to a minister. For too long a time
members have said it around the corridors, have said it in the cafeteria, have said it on the streets, but they do not say it in parliament because they fear they will not be reelected. The people of the Fraser valley think that the labourer is worthy of his hire, and I have no hesitation about saying what I think in public. If I had, I should not be the member for Fraser Valley. It is all utter nonsense to say that a man has any hope of being a member of parliament, let alone an undersecretary, or, above all, attaining to the seats of the mighty in the cabinet under the present system.
I think it is an excellent idea to have assistants to the ministers. Many of the ministers have far too much work to do. They have to spend too much time in the house when they should be carrying on the war effort of Canada. They should not have to be here to answer questions put by myself and other members.
A deputy should be capable of answering these questions, and these deputies should be answering them rather than the ministers. Give . these deputies $8,000, give them $10,000, I do not care what it is, provided that we get results.
Members of parliament should have the courage of their convictions. I can look every party and group in the face when I say that. Apparently many hon. members are afraid to say in the House of Commons what they say around the corridors; they do not want to do that because it goes in Hansard. I was told by a good authority, a man who has been in political life just as long as anyone else in Canada, a man who happens to be in public life to-day, that it is his opinion that we should have this.
We have heard about the franking privilege, and we have heard about other privileges that we have. I am perfectly well aware that what I say now is going back to my riding. Yesterday I answered three telegrams and I had to pay $3.90 of my own money. The government did not pay for those; I did. The people in my riding do not know that. I must pay income tax on the $3.90 that I spent on those telegrams. Why not have the courage of our convictions? Why should we try to hide behind the man who apparently is afraid to stand up for his rights as a member of parliament? I am all for this.
I had nothing to say about the appointment of these assistants. They appear to be excellent men. We over here have heard certain names mentioned and we think we know who will have the appointments. We know some of them and we think they will be excellent

But I cannot justify to the farmers in my riding the fact that we are taxing men in the merchant marine who have to use their feet as bait in order to catch a shark, according to last night's press. I can justify anything in my riding provided that it is helping to win the war. But I will not be able to satisfy my people if I am afraid to come out in the open and state the entire truth of a matter. Is this going to be exempt from income tax?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: My hon. friend asked a very simple question,-whether the appointments which are being made are being made to continue indefinitely, or for a specified time. My hon. friend realizes, I am sure, that we vote supply only for one year and appointments cannot therefore run on more than a year without additional supply being voted. If these appointments are to be continued another year, this house another year will have to vote supply for the purpose. I made it clear, I think, in my introductory remarks that the government was proceeding deliberately in that way to give an opportunity to test out the advantages and also to see if there were disadvantages with respect to the appointment of assistants to the ministers. If, as I hope and believe will prove to be the case, the institution of parliamentary assistants is shown to be highly-beneficial, a bill, I should trust, will later be introduced setting forth specifically the duties of a position which will become a regular part of our parliamentary institutions.

On several occasions
reference has been made to the fact that this item of $40,000 will not fully meet the necessities of the case. There are bound, I would think, to be other expenses, secretarial and so forth. Can the Prime Minister foresee at all what these expenditures will be, and out of what vote he anticipates making them, and if the legislative vote is at the present time not sufficient for that purpose does he foresee a supplementary item?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I think the view of my colleagues is entirely the same as my own. These gentlemen will be provided, in the department with which they may be associated, with accommodation where they can have at least a certain amount of privacy for purposes of their work; they will be given some form of secretarial assistance selected probably from a member of the existing staff. They will carry on in as limited a way as may be adequate for their duties, provision' for this being made out of the general expenses of the department. H it should appear that what we have in

the way of general expenses is inadequate, the house will be asked to make some supplementary addition,. I do not expect there will be much in. the way of additional expense

I would like to take advantage of this opportunity to make a few remarks which I tried to make yesterday afternoon, and when I had to give way to an hon. member from the "middle east", one of the group whose influence with the government and government officials seems to be rather out of proportion to their numerical importance.
As regards the question before us, I remember that the Prime Minister inaugurated this policy of assistants as far back as 1921. I believed in that policy then and I believe in it now. The success of it will, however, depend very largely on the personalities of the men appointed. If they are to be only a sort of fifth wheel, another private secretary, having subordinates under him and getting the idea which some private secretaries do have, that they are of more importance than the ministers, then it will be a failure. Some of these men may not be any better than the admirable private secretaries whom some of the cabinet have at the present time. There are some of them, mostly ladies, as I recall, who must be almost indispensable. They are of the greatest help to the minister and to members of parliament. I have been ashamed in the last two or three years to go and insist upon seeing a cabinet minister because I knew how busy he was, and I tried to do what business I had with subordinates, very often with the private secretary, who proved most useful and accommodating. On the other hand I have known private secretaries who come under neither definition. I recall some time ago going to the private secretary of one of the many cabinet ministers, and his secretary, that is the secretary's secretary, told me that the secretary was engaged and could not see me; he was engaged in the next room. I thought I would just stay there and see how long I would have to wait. I waited three-quarters of an hour; and, from the sounds of amusement which came through the door or the wall, I got the idea that it was not very important public business which was being transacted. At the end of three-quarters of an hour I was permitted to see the minister's secretary. He flipped a book in front of him and said that he might be able to give me an interview with the minister the following Tuesday. This was about Thursday. I said no, I had been waiting three-quarters of an hour and I wanted to see the minister, and I thought members of parliament had a sort of right of way. He said, "No, next Tuesday is the best I can do." I came down to the house
and spoke to the cabinet minister; and he said, "Certainly, I should be glad to see you; come up right now"; and in five minutes he transacted the business wholly to my satisfaction and presumably to his own. If we are to have some more of these extra men who must be placated and bowed down to before one can see the minister or even his secretary, we shall not be much better off than we are now. But if the parliamentary assistant is to be what I hope he will be, able to ease the busy moments of the minister and be readily accessible to members of parliament, it will be a very good thing indeed. I hope that is what will happen and that the experiment will be a real success.
I was in favour of the proposal when the Prime Minister said he would have to have the appointment of these secretaries. Some people have suggested that the individual ministers should appoint them. But, after all, the Prime Minister is head of the government, and I think that, as such, he should have the duty and the responsibility of appointing them. I also agreed with him when he said he thought he would have to select a man acceptable to the minister. Naturally he could not expect two men to pull together if they were not congenial to each other. But I entirely differed from him when he went on to say that he felt that the man appointed must be not only acceptable to him-which is quite all right-and not only acceptable to the minister-which also is all right-but acceptable to the deputy minister. I entirely differ from that.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I think that point is being overemphasized. What I had in mind was that the minister would find it impossible to have as his assistant someone who, for example, was antagonistic to his deputy. This is just a matter of taking human nature into consideration. I would not want it to be thought I was saying that the deputy of the departments should be consulted, and that his wishes must necessarily be met. All I had in mind when I said what I did was that the assistant to the minister should be a person with whom the permanent head of the department could work. Otheiwise his own value would be greatly impaired.

That is exactly what I said, and it is exactly what Hansard reveals the Prime Minister said, namely that the man appointed has to be acceptable to the deputy. Presumably the Prime Minister must ascertain the opinion of the deputy minister. I know of no deputy minister with whom in many years past I have not been on the best of terms; so that I have no grievance from that point of view. But if I am a young man coming into parliament, if I am ambitious and wish to have success, I

must not only secure the approval and the good will of the Prime Minister-and properly so-and of the ministers, but I have also to secure the approval of the deputy ministers.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No, no. That is not at all what is implied.

They have to approve. I have to secure their favour before I can qualify for a position. The deputy minister is a civil servant, and I am a member of parliament. It is not the duty of a member of parliament to secure further advancement through the good will of a deputy minister. I repeat that I have every good will for deputy ministers; I have never had trouble with them. Nevertheless, as I say they are civil servants; they are not members of parliament. The Prime Minister has now said that the would-be aspirant must have thq approval of the deputy minister. If I have some reason to complain respecting the actions of a deputy minister, I must suppress my views, I must conceal them for fear a black mark would be raised against me in days to come. And this procedure is also placing the deputy minister in a peculiar position. To be dragged into politics is the last thing in God's world they want.
As we know, deputy ministers continue in office from cabinet to cabinet. They are not fired when governments change, nor should they be. They must carry out the policies of the minister of the moment. When one minister leaves office, upon a change of government, and another minister takes hold, the one who is taking office gets just as loyal service from the deputy who has given loyal service to the one who is leaving office. We find less difficulty in that regard here in Ottawa than is found in the country. When a political appointment is wanted one finds it generally comes from back home, rather than from the official head of the department. That is how they continue to give good service. For example, let us take a man like the late Mr. Hunter, of the Department of Public Works. Would he have desired to be dragged into a position where he would have to express an opinion as to whether so-and-so or so-and-so should act as assistant to the minister? If the deputy minister is going to do that, then why not let him have a say as to who should be elected as a member? I must object to that feature.
I suggest also that the appointment should be made by an act or, as it is said, by a bill. When the Prime Minister seeks to change any department it has always been the practice to have a bill introduced. When the Department of Munitions and Supply was set up some years ago a bill which set out the duties and scope of operation was introduced.
(Mr. Neill.]
But here are men appointed only through an item in the estimates, and I say it is a most peculiar way of doing it. It would have been much better if it had been by an act, even though of .a temporary character. It would have been quite easy to pass a bill and have these assistants appointed in the regular way. We could have discussed and defined, their duties and powers; all those matters would have been clearly understood, and probably such procedure would have led to a better and happier operation of the positions later on.
While I am on my feet I should like to ask the Prime Minister-'and this is purely a matter of curiosity-why it was necessary at this late date, before the Easter adjournment, when we have to rush business through, to have this one item of the estimates forced through to make provision for the pay of these new appointments. Is the government in the position of the Chinaman who said he would not work unless he got his money beforehand? If the Prime Minister had risen in his seat and said that he had arranged for the appointment of these gentlemen as parliamentary assistants, we would1 have allowed them to act. We would have accepted their positions, and payment of money to them could have been arranged in the usual way, through the estimates. I cannot understand why it was necessary to rush this one item of the estimates through at this time, by itself. It would have been much better if it had been done by way of a bill.
Perhaps in what I am about to say I shall be a little out of order. However, the previous speaker was allowed to introduce a matter which was not strictly in order, and I should like to say a few words respecting the remarks of the hon. member for Fraser Valley. Whatever I might think of his sentiments. I admire his courage. As he says, he has been ventilating in the house what has been undoubtedly common gossip for months and months. I do not think he explained it quite as clearly as he might have. The position is this-and I know I am speaking to the country as well as to the committee. Members of parliament are paid1 $4,000 indemnity. Deputy ministers are paid either $9,000 or $10,000, according to years of service. As a private citizen, the deputy minister can spend his money in any way he wishes. But the $4,000 we get for our services is, in large part, only a gesture. [DOT] We do not get [DOT]that S4.000; we get only a small portion of it. We are compelled as members of parliament to incur large expenditures-and very properly. It may be said that we knew about all

these obligations before we took the job, and that if we do not want our jobs other people will be glad to have them. All that may be so. I am not asking for any more salary, and I do not care what the taxation is, provided that I am treated fairly and squarely; but I do object to paying taxes on money I never saw, and never put into my pocket.
The expense of living in Ottawa is enormous in these days. Then we have expenses of travel. When I am home I have to have an office. If it were not my own office I would have to pay rent for it. I must pay charges for electric light and telephone, and I must keep a stenographer solely for political business. All these expenses come out of the $4,000. And there are other expenses as well. We must travel through our constituencies. The cost of living in Ottawa is much greater than that of living at home, and we must maintain two households. If I were in any other occupation whatsoever-if for instance I were a lawyer-and had to make returns of income I would be allowed, without a particle of doubt, to deduct from my gross income the expense of getting it. I would be permitted to deduct what I pay a stenographer in my office, and all the expenses connected therewith. But when it comes to being a member of parliament-oh, no; those expenses are supposed to come from some unknown source, and cannot be allowed as expenses incurred in connection with getting one's income.
For many years the legislature of British Columbia allowed its members to write off $2,000 against their income, for purposes of taxation. They did not have to itemize it, or anything else, but just took the $2,000 off their gross income before being charged income tax. Some years ago that was changed to $1,000. Of course in British Columbia we have now lost that privilege because income tax is taken away from the province and given to the federal government.
At one time, more for purposes of getting information than anything else, for one solid year I kept an account of my expenses, what it cost me in various ways, outside of actual living and personal expenses. I did not charge those, because I would have had to incur them anyhow. I made a fairly close check of it and I found that at the end of the year, after deducting the fair and necessary expenses of being a member, I had $1,100 left, and it would be much less now, and yet I am told that for taxation purposes I am to be assessed on the whole S4.000. I took up this point fifteen years ago with one of the officials of the department. I pointed to the clause in the act which says expenses should be allowed to 72537-1531
anyone who, in connection with his occupation or business, must be away from home. The official replied, "Yes, but being a member of parliament is not an occupation." I said I thought it was, but if not it was a business, but he said no. I then asked what it was, and he said it was an honour and therefore these expenses could not be deducted. In later years, since taxation has gone up, some hon. members approached another official, but he simply laughed and said, "No doubt you are right, but you have been fools enough to put up with it all these years."
Then the hon. member for Fraser Valley touched upon a point which does come home to us all. It is suggested that this might not be a very opportune time to go home to our constituents-if we have an eye towards the next election-and say, "We have reached out our hand and taxed you people heavily, but we have taken advantage of our power to cut down our own taxation." However, while that may sound plausible, and while no doubt it would be used by our opponents, the hon. member for Fraser Valley said he was not afraid of his constituents, and neither am I afraid of mine. The working man, the union man, the small wage-earner to whom you would put that specious argument of taxing him and not taxing yourself, is intelligent and reasonable. I think he would quite readily understand and agree that if we did our best to get justice for him here it would be all right for us to get justice for ourselves. I do not think there would be any danger on that account. Some people have a poor idea of the intelligence of what they scornfully call the common people. I will trust the common people every time. Let me remind the house of an incident that occurred some years ago, to show how the union man and; the wage-earner looks at these things. A provincial government in Nova Scotia was facing an-election, and the ministers thought they might make themselves popular and appeal to the working men and small wage-earners by cutting down their own salaries by a considerable amount, some $300 or $400. The next day they looked anxiously and hopefully at the newspapers, and the labour paper came out with a great big headline saying "Legislators Reduce Their Own Salaries." Underneath in slightly smaller print was the comment of the newspaper: "Cheap skates; they know their own value." That was all they got by playing politics and thinking they were going to help themselves in that way.
I think that is about all I have to say on this point. At the moment perhaps it would not be politic to take this action, since some people might look at it from the wrong point

of view. As I see it, however, we have been unfairly treated. Now we are being taxed heavily, something like 40 or 50 per cent, on money we never see, money fairly and lawfully spent in order to obtain our salaries as members, which we know we are entitled to deduct for income tax purposes just as the working man or business man or anyone else may deduct his necessary expenses incurred in obtaining his gross income.
And serving our constituents as well.

Absolutely. I remember one gentleman who sat beside me in the local house many years ago, who sent down and got some office equipment. I asked1, "What do you want that for? You do not need it." His reply was, "Well, Neill, I am entitled to that, and, if I cannot be trusted to look after my own interests, how can I be trusted to look after the interests of my constituents?" I do think that to uphold the dignity of Canada and to give to the Prime Minister the place he should have in entertainment and in many ways requiring outlays from his pocket, his remuneration should be adequate to the place that Canada holds among the nations of the world. ,
I a.m amazed that there should be any divergence of opinion with regard to the services that can be rendered by parliamentary assistants. Vision is essential to progress, and the addition of members of this parliament to continuous service amongst the various departments will be bringing to these departments new vision and enhancing the parliamentary control that is so much demanded right across the country. It is totally impossible for a minister in one of the large departments to keep in close contact with the many thousands of men and women in the service which he is administering. Human nature is human nature; many things that should come to the attention of the minister may at times be covered up, and I should think that if the parliamentary assistant is of the right type and possessed of a ferreting mind his very presence may instil into some persons in the service a fear that their sloppiness of method or their disregard for public money may be uncovered. I consider that it would be a sound investment to have capable men serving the ministers of busy departments, for there is no doubt they will more than pay for themselves.
I am sure that the youth of this country and those of democratic spirit and ideals will expect this parliament to enlarge the scope of its usefulness and not to suffer the restrictions that are imposed upon it through some who are permanently in the service as our hired servants. We have a splendid body of highly trained and efficient men and women in the service, and again we have others who may not be so competent. I am sure that the addition of some representatives from this parliament as parliamentary assistants will in the end save money to the country and bring about increased efficiency.

I am in accord with some of the observations made by the hon. member for Davenport. I concur in what he said with regard to the civil service of Canada. I am thinking particularly of the portion of the civil service which has to do with the Department of Finance. I have criticized, and criticized rather strongly, some of the incumbents of high office in the Department of Finance, thinking that their minds run in the realm of philosophy and conjecture through their early training in professorships and what-not rather than in the world of business. To assist the minister and his department I have been concerned for some time as to why the government has not seen fit to fill the posts now vacant in the Department of Finance and so relieve the minister of some of his burdens. An outstanding example is the position known as the commissioner of tariffs. The minister very properly takes the view that during a time of war this is a matter that should be left as is. I agree with him, and I think he will admit that he is getting the maximum of cooperation from all those concerned with that particular office and the functioning of that work. But at the same time, business is going on; that department is Still functioning, and matters which would ordinarily be disposed of by the commissioner of tariffs now have to come to the minister or to some of his deputies, and necessarily he takes the responsibility and is loaded with that extra burden. True, the previous incumbent, one of the most capable civil servants Canada has had for a long time, is functioning as president of the stabilization corporation, and undoubtedly is giving a good account of himself. He has a tremendous task; he cannot be diverted from it. In my opinion it is one of the most responsible appointments in the civil service of Canada to-day. It has to do with fighting inflation; millions of dollars are being worked out in debits and credits to one industry and another in order to hold down the cost of living and all that goes with it

The house resumed from Tuesday, April 20, consideration in committee of Bill No. 72, to amend the Income War Tax Act-Mr. Ilsley- Mr. Bradette in the chair.
On section 13-1942 individual reduced tax liability.

Just prior to the adjournment last night I was making a few remarks on this section. While I regret having to harass the minister at this time, in view of the necessity of getting this bill through as quickly as possible, there are a few thoughts which I should like to leave with him over the recess with respect to income tax deductions, particularly as applied to industrial workers. My reason for bringing up this matter is a telegram which I received from the steel workers union, Sydney, Nova Scotia, dated April 20. It represents the view of some 5,000 workers and it reads:
Sydney steel workers union in regular session after lengthy consideration present widespread criticism income tax deduction scales. Respectfully urge revisions so that maximum deductions shall be limited to forty-eight hours' earnings each week.
I know this particular body of -men, and there is no more reasonable group in Canada.
I do not think there is a more efficient organization in the trade union movement in this country. When these officials send a telegram like that I know that there must be serious criticism by the membership of these income tax deductions. A revised table of tax deductions was issued by the department for March 31, 1943. I should like to suggest something which I think will offset the present resentment against these deductions.
I take as an example a single man earning 832 a week, which gives him an income of

Income War Tax
SI,660 a year, working a 48 hour week. The tax rate places him in the 30 per cent bracket for the first S500 and1 in the 33 per cent bracket for the balance. His tax deduction is $7.90 per week, S2.45 of which is refundable. This leaves him a net of $24.10 per week. The point I should like to make with respect to this particular man would apply to most of the employees in plants and factories across Canada.
There is an urgency in war work in steel plants, ship repair plants and shipbuilding plants. I think it will be admitted that a 48 hour week is about all that a man should be obliged to work. However, there is a necessity for overtime work because of war emergencies. It is a common thing for the employer, the personnel manager or the plant manager to come to a group of employees in the middle of the week or at the end of the week and say, "A ship has come in with a hole in her; there is an emergency job to be done, and we want you men to stay on this week-end." Those men may work three shifts over the week-end. Under their contract they are paid time and a half for overtime. Take the particular man I have cited. If he is willing to give up his leisure over the week-end and take the punishment of additional work, something the average man does not want to do, he will increase his earnings to $56 for that week. This higher wage takes him out of the income bracket he was in before, and his deduction. instead of being $7.90 will be $18.65, of which $4.25 is savings. His net balance will be $37.35. His tax deduction has been increased $10.75. The point I wish to make is that instead of his being in the income bracket of 30 and 33 per cent, he now finds himself in the 41 per cent bracket.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Only on a little bit at the top.
No.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It does not run back into the whole thing.

It takes in the total earnings. The minister has in mind the fact that the_ schedules are computed on the basis of yearly earnings, but this tax is being deducted on a weekly basis. The worker's gross income for the week determines the income tax bracket he will be in for that week. I know what the minister is thinking of

that the total income tax can be figured out at the end of the year and if there has been too much taken off in weekly deductions application can be made for a refund. But I am pointing out the actual situation, that present conditions make this a sore spot, and that the effect of the whole thing is for the man to hold back
because he feels that in working extra time he is punishing himself. Many of these men put on their working clothes and do not get home till the end of the week. In addition to taking that physical punishment, if they work long hours they are placed in a different income tax group for that week, and the net result is for them to feel that they do not want to take on extra work. That is how the steel worker feels. That is the single man in the low income group. On top of that, you have increased the deductions this year by some 25 per cent over last year. That was not expected; it has not been thoroughly explained, and naturally in all the big industries across Canada there is resentment against the income tax.
What can be done about it? I think the whole matter should be closely examined. If you are going to get your emergency war work done on the basis of extra time, you might well exclude for income tax purposes anything the man may make by way of overtime in contributing to the country's war effort in such an emergency. If you do not want to go that far, this might be considered, that the income tax of the worker shall be based on his 48-hour week; and if he puts in overtime, do not change the rate of taxation by applying the rate to his higher earnings, but apply the 30 and 33 per cent to his entire earnings for that week and leave him in the income group he is in at the present time.
I leave these thoughts with the minister because I know there is terrific resentment against the taxing arrangements.
I think somebody in the department has badly neglected1 the matter of publicity with respect to the savings portion of the tax. It is not generally understood. By and large, when the men get their pay envelopes they will look at the deductions and think that they amount to straight taxation. There is nothing to indicate that a certain portion of the deduction is refundable after the war. I have received several letters suggesting that the pay forms should be so drawn as to inform the man that he is paying so much by way of tax and that so much will be refundable, that the tax and the refundable portion are two separate items. That should be set out on the pay slip. There should be a record of it so that the worker will have a clear understanding that in the event of his death the refundable portion of his tax will be paid to his estate, or if he lives it will be paid to himself two years after the war. That is another point on which the workers are confused. Their general complaint is that they have nothing to show that a certain portion of the tax is refundable. It might not be a bad
Income War Tax

idea once a month, or every quarter or every six months, whichever the department considers most convenient, to issue a certificate to the worker showing what portion of his deductions is refundable. The department should issue a certificate to the man who is making that contribution, setting out clearly that he has that much money on deposit with the government and that it will be refundable after the war.
The psychological effect of making that clear to the worker is the most important job that the department has to do to-day. The letters I have received about the matter do not complain about paying the tax, but they deprecate the fact that the worker is not given a certificate showing what he has to his credit. There is nothing on their pay envelope to indicate that anything will be refunded when the war is over, or that if he dies in the meantime the money will be paid to his widow or his estate. These are matters which should be considered by the department, because they are causing a lot of complaint.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am very much obliged to the hon. gentleman for his suggestions. I realize that he has put his finger on two problems. One is how to arrange our income tax that it does not discourage overtime and perhaps to a certain extent discourage working every day in the week. I shall have to give consideration to his suggestions. There has been, as he knows, a great deal of discussion of that problem here during the last two weeks. The financial critic of the opposition dealt with it very fully in his speech, and other members have dealt with it. It is something for which we shall have to try to get a remedy if we possibly can.
The other problem is also an acute one.
I have tried to make it clear every time I have spoken on the subject that the refundable portion of the tax will be repaid, with two per cent interest, within two years after the war, and if the taxpayer dies in the meantime it will become payable at once to his estate. I have prepared a very emphatic passage from my budget speech on that, with a view to making the facts known as widely as possible, but it is very hard to get proper publicity f<jr these matters.
That does not touch the other question, which is whether the employee should not receive something, not from the government, but from the employer as he goes along, showing what he has to his credit in refundable savings. This matter has been giving us a great deal of concern ever since last September. Certain representatives of organized labour made representations to us 
last September that that should be done, otherwise the employee would have nothing to show and would think his money was simply gone and he would never get it back. There have been recent attempts by regulation by the Department of National Revenue to oblige the employers to give statements to the employees in certain contingencies. That is, when the year is up, and when the employee leaves his employ, he is entitled to a statement of what has been deducted and what is refundable. The reason why it is not possible to give a certificate of the amount of refundable taxes with every payroll period is that the amount of refundable taxes depends to some extent upon the man's yearly earnings. Therefore the amount deducted on account of refundable taxes is not conclusive. Consequently, if certificates were given that that much was there as refundable taxes, they might add up to too much at the end of the year; there might be some adjustment necessary; and then, of course, the employer or the government or both would be in trouble, because the employee would have the certificates and he would say: "Where *is my money?"
But that is the result of a system of taxation, is it not? It is by reason of the collection on weekly basis that exists.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is right.
And if you did not tax any higher than on ordinary rates of pay, that would not occur.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Oh, it would occur, because there is not complete regularity of employment. All I can say to members of the committee about the matter is that nobody realizes more clearly than I do that these are real, difficult and important problems, and that the solution of these two problems would help in the war effort a great'deal. We shall just have to give the best consideration to them that we can.

speechtext: Yes; it applies to 1942. But the regulation was not passed before the end of the year. I will ask the Minister of National Revenue to explain it.

At the end of the year the employer must file a return showing the names of his employees and the amount of compulsory savings and tax that he has taken from each employee. That was to have been filed in September of this year, because the employer was collecting from the employee on the basis of tax collection for the whole of last year. The deductions from salary or wages have to be made on a form that the employee makes out, and when he makes application for a refund he has to fill out form T.D. 20A. It seems to me that the trouble about this form-I objected to it about two years ago when it was brought in-is, in the first place, that about 90 per cent of the employees are not fitted to do this kind of work; they are not temperamentally suited to it; many of them do not like the job of filling out all these forms, and they would rather let the money go than bother to ask for a refund. They have to get a certificate from their employer stating how much is deducted from their wages, whether the wages are paid weekly, monthly or otherwise, and give full particulars, and then they have to sign it. On the other side, the man is forced to state his name and the address to which the refund cheque is to be mailed. The case I took up a couple of years ago was a test case. This chap had earned for a short period, enough to bring him within the income tax group. At the end of the year his income was less than SI,100, with the result that any deductions from his pay by way of taxes were refundable. But by the time he got down all the names of his employers for the whole year and their addresses he had a considerable difficulty. One of his employers happened to have died in the meantime. We chased this thing through the department for about eighteen months, and then gave it up as a bad job.

My opinion is that experience would be that about 90 per cent of those entitled to this refund would never obtain the deduction.
That is not a compliment to the people, you know.

speechtext: The two per cent is free of income tax. It is a very generous rate.

I take a contrary view of this whole section to that taken by the department. In the first place the failure to treat those who receive investment incomes above $3,000 on the same basis as that on which everyone else is treated, even executives with $10,000 to $50,000 salary, is not -understandable to many people. It was always felt that those -who had large incomes were taxed and that adequate recognition had been given in previous budgets to their ability to pay. I hardly think the minister would deny that ability to pay had been a factor that was given thorough consideration. He would have considered himself remiss if it had not been given adequate consideration.
A second point which I do not think was brought out particularly when the resolution was under discussion has to do with the fact that these investment incomes are derived largely through investments in companies on which a minimum tax of forty per cent is paid even on pre-war scale earnings, so that there is a very heavy rate of tax even before the people get any share of the earnings, which in turn is subject to personal income tax. In addition to that, as if these two taxes were not enough, a four per cent surtax on investment income is added to the other taxes which the individual must pay. It would seem to me,

Income War Tax
therefore, that if the minister cannot concede the main point he might at least have allowed these people the same rate on the prepayment of their tax-which again I claim is a third succession duty-at the going rate for government money, namely, three per cent. However, I do not expect to get, in this budget, very much relief for taxpayers, particularly in this bracket.
But I wish to ask this question. We have a great many sections of the income tax bill to review before we adjourn for the recess. If we are to adjourn at six o'clock until May 6 we shall have to go over matters very hurriedly. If, on the other hand, the minister- and the Prime Minister perhaps-is to be insistent upon our sitting after six o'clock-of course I realize it is only by unanimous consent that we can be asked to sit after six o'clock-I should like to know from the Minister of Finance just what the wish of the department is and what the reasons are behind that wish, because if hon. members are to be asked to give unanimous consent to these matters I think we should know precisely why there is this frightful rush to put the bill through and have it enacted. As we have seen, there have been, not only many discussions between the Minister of Finance and the Minister of National Revenue on these various points, but many discussions with their deputies. With some of these matters they are not as familiar as they might be. They themselves have caused this house much more delay than private members have done. This shows once again that when we have such vital matters before us affecting the Canadian public as we have in modern budgets the only proper way is to have a committee where there can be cross-examination, where the ministers can develop their ideas and where hon. members can present and develop their own ideas and find out such things as they and the public require to know. Consequently I would ask the minister what are his plans for the afternoon and what are his desires for the evening, if it is necessary to sit after the dinner recess, because this will make some difference in our discussions of these various matters. If we are to be forced to get through with this bill at some time this evening there is no use in reiterating any arguments which have been brought up before or in asking the minister to make any concessions. We know he probably will not make any concessions, despite the fact that in his budget speech he said these resolutions were only recommendations to the house. I must say that I have seen very little changed here, no matter what arguments were advanced or what viewpoints
were expressed. I could mention four or five matters dealt with in previous budgets in connection with which we did argue quite strenuously; sometimes the minister became very heated at the time, but later, in subsequent budgets, he actually made the changes or gave effect to the suggestions that were advocated by the opposition.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I hope to get through with this bill this afternoon.
And if we do not?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not know. The question is whether- w-e should sit to-night, and I shall have to consult the Prime Minister and see whether he is willing to go on to-night.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The urgency is that we have a sessional programme of tremendous scope and extent, and unless we fix some time for getting through certain parts of that programme it will become almost impossible to finish it. It has already received an enormous amount of consideration, and I do not think we ought to plan to come back and go into this bill again, but I am in the hands of the committee on that. I am only anxious to get it through. There is the mutual aid bill, which is most pressing; we have not touched the war appropriation at all; we have hardly touched any estimates at all, and there is a great deal of other legislation. Hon. members are bringing up matters all the time and saying they are urgent, and I think we ought to try to put this bill through this afternoon.

The need is general
rather than specific, then, in connection with all these bills.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Well, if there were any possibility of this being changed it would be very serious, and if there is no possibility of it being changed we might as well put it through. The Department of National Revenue has to get out its forms; employers are at the present time making the deductions under this scheme, and it is most important that we know at a very early date what the law is. I cannot discuss in detail what would be the effect upon the revenue department if we did not get through with this bill to-day. I suppose they would just have to send out the forms on the assumption that the bill would not be changed. They
Income War Tax

did that once, and they were savagely attacked in this house for it; they were asked what right in the world they had to do such a bureaucratic thing. Well, they have to do that bureaucratic thing, or else they have to get some legislation behind them.

I wish to say just a w'ord in relation to paragraph (b) of section 9A, having to do with the date of the deferred payments, which is set at April 30, 1944. Perhaps that date should be extended, for the reason that taxation is now the heaviest it has been, and probably the heaviest it is likely to be for a great number of years. If one wants to make that deferred payment and the date is set arbitrarily at April 30, 1944, it imposes on the taxpayer an obligation during the fiscal year 1943-44 which will be a hardship to a great number of people.-I suggest that as the section stands not many people are likely to take advantage of the discount of two per cent in making that deferred payment.
I wonder whether the officials of the department have given consideration to this aspect. Suppose a person's income tax is $20,000, of which $10,000 is deferred. He can make an arrangement prior to April, 1944, in regard to that payment, Suppose he arranges that the payment is to be made by his estate after his death. Then it becomes a liability against his estate and will be deducted from it. It stands to reason that as a result his estate will not pay succession duties on that $10,000. If he sees that as I do, his estate will be money ahead by not taking advantage of the deferment. My suggestion is that if the date is put back to 1946 or 1948, or even five years further, many people will take advantage of it and have the matter cleared up, and the government will be money in pocket in that they will get succession duties on the amounts represented by those deferred payments.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We gave much consideration to the selection of that date and finally decided that April 30, 1944, was the most appropriate date. It is a year. A person taking advantage of the prepayment and the discount can do so either in whole or in part, it will be noted from the section. The further the date is extended, the greater the opportunity to choose an option prejudicial to the crown.
I would be interested to see in this bill anything that is prejudicial to the crown.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The basis of the section is that the income tax payable on investment
[Mr. Hsley.l
income beyond the first $3,000 is payable on the death of the taxpayer, by his estate. He is given a chance under this section to discount that on the basis of expectancy of life, and naturally if he can find out something about his actual expectancy of life, and it is not great, he will avail himself of the discount. If it is in fact two years but the tables give him twenty years, he will take advantage of the discount.
The minister is taking it for granted, I assume, that the expectancy of these people, whether because of fright or for other reasons, will be about a year?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No; lam not taking anything for granted, but I know that those whose actual expectancy is very much shorter than their mortality table expectancy will be the ones who will choose this system, while the others will not. The moment that fact sinks into the consciousness of the people, it becomes apparent that you must fix a fairly early date. If you made it 1946 or 1948 you would get a greatly increased scope for that choice, with the risk against the crown.
What about the other question I asked, in regard to succession duties? I suggested that the crown would lose money in succession duties. Is that correct?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes; that is correct. If the payment is made by the estate on the taxpayer's death, it escapes succession duties on that amount, which is deducted from the estate. If the taxpayer paid it before death, however, his estate would be reduced accordingly, perhaps not to so great an extent but at least to the extent of the payment. He will just have to select the alternative that he thinks is most advantageous to him.
By the way, I should like to say something about what was said by the hon. member for Rosedale the other day, when he pointed out that the older the man, the higher would be the tax. The older the man, the greater the relief would be without the tax. That is the answer, because in effect if we suppose the whole tax were forgiven, it would really be a relief of the estate. Substantially it is a relief of the estate, and if that relief is coming in two years it is worth much more than if it came in twenty years. So that the old man is not discriminated against, as compared with the younger man.

In view of the admission the minister has made in connection with my question respecting succession duties, is it not a fact that in the long run the crown stands to lose something by this arrangement?

Income War Tax

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Oh no, it does not, unless this process of selection against the crown takes place. That is the reason for the early date.
Mr. MeCANN: That is why it is likely to.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If you extend the date, then that really does get the crown into trouble, comparatively speaking, because it gives that many more years for this selection to take place. Let us suppose the hon. member owed a 810,000 tax, payable upon his death out of his estate, and he discovers in 1945 that his expectancy of life is not great. He immediately takes advantage of the assessment, does he not, because his mortality table expectancy of life is probably, normally, twenty or thirty years? He finds out that his real expectancy is only four or five years, and therefore immediately takes advantage of the situation. If he has to make an election within a year, between now and 1944, there is not nearly as much selection. The mortality tables are based on the assumption that everybody took advantage of the discount system, at once. But when part can, and part cannot, it is important that the ones who can be put to their election as early as possible. '

Would the Minister of National Revenue give some further information respecting acknowledgments employers have .to give employees in respect of compulsory savings? If I understood him correctly, he said that such acknowledgment, by regulation, would have to be given some time this year-May or June-for 1942. Is the acknowledgment to be part of that long, thin slip the employers give to the employees, or is it to be in some other form? Individual slips are torn off and given by employers to their employees, stating annual income and various deductions which have been made. Is there an item in the new form which covers compulsory savings, or is there something else?

Four copies of the form are to be completed, two of which go to the department, one being retained by the employer and the other, containing the information, is given to the employee. So that when the form is prepared there are four copies available.
And if is about that form you are speaking when you make reference to the amount of compulsory savings deducted by employers?

The employer informs the government respecting the total amount he has deducted. The amount that is credited to compulsory savings cannot be definitely determined until the tax returns have been filed by employees, and the assessment made.
No one can determine exactly what the compulsory savings are, from each weekly payment. The table of tax deductions shows the total tax, and the compulsory savings portion. That compulsory savings portion _ is there so that if an employee has offsetting savings, the employer knows he can deduct from the total tax payable the amount of savings made by the taxpayer, up to the amount of the refundable portion of the tax as shown on the table. That is the reason why the two are shown.
Consequently the tax the employer holds back from the pay, and turns in to the government, is the total amount of tax, less any deduction to which the employee is entitled on account of personal savings he may have made through mortgages, and life insurance up to the amount of the savings portion.

I should like to be clear on the statement the minister made that by a regulation recently passed employers were compelled, or obliged, to make a statement respecting their employees, in respect of two conditions the minister mentioned. One was with respect to the termination of employment, and the other was at the end of the calendar year. When I asked a supplementary question the reply was that it referred to 1942, but that these acknowledgments had not yet been given, and that they would be given after the report was made. I believe the minister mentioned either May or June.
Yes; companies have not yet filed them for 1942. They are due on May 31.

May I get it clear, then, that employees should look for nothing else from their employers in addition to the slip they get at the end of the year, in which are shown their total receipts for the year, and total deductions?

Yes; that slip must show the amount the employer has sent to the government, and it will be that amount we shall have to check with the employee's return. We will check the employer's return with the amount claimed by the employee when he files his individual return.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I understand that in my absence a question was asked as to the government's intention in the matter of proceeding with this measure later in the day, in the event of discussion not being concluded by six o'clock.
Let me say the government had hoped we might have cleared the order paper of all the items other than those relating immediately to the war and to supply, before the Easter recess. It is now obvious, if we are to adjourn

Income War Tax
immediately after the assent to bills it is not going to be possible to have any discussion on the two notices respecting committees, one in connection with radio broadcasting and the other, war-time expenditures. I believe we shall have to forgo consideration of them before adjournment of the Easter recess.
But with respect to this measure, the Income War Tax Act, the government would like very much to have it concluded before we adjourn for the Easter recess. May I say it is not the intention to ask hon. members, when once it passes this chamber, to wait until this bill has been considered in another place. What we are concerned about is that when the house reassembles on May 6 we may, from that time forward, proceed with war measures, and not have the attention of hon. members diverted back to a discussion, which might be prolonged, in respect of budget resolutions and bills based thereon. For that reason wre would like to have discussion on this bill concluded so far as this house is concerned before we adjourn'.
At a quarter to. six to-day there is to be an assent to bills which have already passed the house. I should hope it might be possible to conclude the discussion on this measure by that time. But if it is not, might I suggest that hon. members agree to coming back to this chamber immediately after the assent, and continue the discussion on the bill until such discussion is concluded. If that can be agreed upon I think I may say the government will not take up any additional measures after the conclusion of this one. If we came back immediately after six o'clock, it would permit hon. members to have at least a part of the evening free of the house. I hope, however, it may be possible to get through by a quarter to six.

The official opposition is always ready, as the government is aware, to assist in the passage of measures, where there is a clear indication that we shall accomplish something by so working. To my mind the difficulty has to a great extent been caused by heading for a fortnight's adjournment at this time, when so important a measure as this has still to be passed.
We have just about an hour until we shall be called for royal assent. There are sixteen more pages to be considered. The fact that this measure is obviously of the greatest importance can be judged by the discussion which has taken place on the different sections. The previous proceedings were held up largely because of the necessity of amendments which were being made by the government. Having got rid of the majority of the members of the

house, we now find present the faithful few who always stay on to endeavour to assist the government to get its measures through. So far as I can speak for those with me, we are ready to come back after the dinner recess if there is any reasonable hope that we can finish this important measure by eleven o'clock. However, as I say, there are still sixteen pages that have to be discussed.

I agree largely with what the hon. member for Yale has said. There are a large number of sections to be considered, some of them very important. If we are to have the same kind of discussion that took place when the resolution was in committee, we shall need considerable time. We met at two o'clock to-day, and if we rise at six o'clock, come back at eight o'clock and make an attempt to get through before we adjourn to-night, I think hon. members would appreciate the break. The hon. member for Yale has suggested that there are very few members in Ottawa and in the house. Those of us who are here are, I believe, trying to confine what we have to say to the points in which we are particularly interested. That is certainly what we are trying to do. I think we should adjourn at six o'clock for an hour or so in order to come back a little more refreshed than some of us feel just now.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I may say for the government that we appreciate the attitude of the acting leader of the opposition and the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar. So far as the government is concerned we would wish to meet, as far as we are able to, what would best suit the convenience of hon. members. The fact that the house did meet at two o'clock to-day would possibly make it advisable to adjourn at six o'clock immediately after royal assent, and reassemble at seven o'clock rather than at eight.
With the understanding that we sit continuously until we get through; that we be not held up again at midnight but go right on?
Sit until midnight? No.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Come back and sit until the bill is through. That is what the hon. member had.in mind. If the house is agreeable we would resume at eight o'clock.
The hon. member just suggested seven o'clock.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I thought some exception was taken to that. If we could agree on seven o'clock, that would be desirable.
I shall have to put a special motion because of standing order 2 which relates to the sitting of the house on Wednesday night. Mr. Speaker

Income War Tax
will have to be in the chair before I can put the motion. I would say to my hon. friend opposite that this government measure has not been delayed because it has not been brought forward by the government as rapidly as possible. As my hon. friend knows, there has been a discussion of many matters which has occupied a good deal of time before these measures could be reached. I mention that only because I want to make it clear that there has not been any negligence or delay on the' part of the government in bringing the measure forward. May I say also that I would not make the request I am now making if there had not been in the discussion on the resolutions a very full consideration of the matters to be taken up.
Progress reported.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
By leave of the house I move:
That the house be not adjourned at six o'clock to-day, but that its sitting be then suspended until seven o'clock p.m. when it will be resumed under the same rule as at eight o'clock on other days.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: Certainly it does.

Certainly it would need unanimous consent at eleven o'clock. I am ready to meet the wishes of the government, so far as I can speak for those with me, that [DOT] we should reassemble at seven o'clock, but I am not agreeable to sitting after eleven o'clock.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I was hoping that the general consensus would be that if we came back at seven o'clock or earlier, having in view the completion of this bill within _ a reasonable time after coming back, it would not be necessary to consider at what hour the adjournment would take place. Certainly it would require unanimous consent if we wished to sit beyond eleven o'clock.

I am sure the Prime Minister does not need to be reminded that it is not so many years ago that this house used to sit all night or late into the night. If it is necessary to get through the legislation now before the house I do not think it would
hurt hon. members to stay here. They are not so delicate that they must go home and go to bed at eleven o'clock, that is, if they do go to bed.

I agree to a large extent with the hon. member for Yukon. I would much prefer having the house rise at six o'clock to reassemble at eight o'clock and then stay on until we have finished this bill. I think a two-hour break would be preferable to one hour. I do not know how the hon. member for Yale and his friends feel, but I would prefer to reassemble at eight o'clock and stay until we have finished.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I think possibly it would be wise to reassemble not later than seven o'clock. We shall thereby be a little more certain of having the extra time that may be necessary'. If the house agrees, we shall reassemble at seven o'clock.
