On section 17-Reference to treasury board.

Once again this is a section which gives the government power to declare illegal that which was legal. I asked the Minister of Finance the other day if he would give us examples of concrete cases which were aimed at in this legislation, and he said it was not his department. I therefore ask the Minister of National Revenue, if the Minister of Finance does not w'ish to take the responsibility for piloting this section through. Surely I have the right to ask some minister what some of the cases are.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am not able to give the hon. gentleman that information. Just see what he is asking! He is asking me to outline types of transactions, many of which are extremely complicated. But the principles laid down here are the principles which underlie the transactions. The type of transaction indicated by subsection 3 is, I think, fairly clear; also the transactions that are governed by the principles of subsection 2.

I think we should protest against this policy of giving the treasury board power to make the law. But I understand that the minister is adamant on putting this section through, and therefore I shall not labour my point further.
The minister-I will not say undertook the other day to give us some of these cases, buL-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I did not give any undertaking.

I did not say he did, but I implied that somebody had and I referred to the Minister of National Revenue as being responsible. I certainly expected to find out what some of the evils aimed at were. The reason why I asked that is that the government is asking for blanket powers to declare that which was legal when it was done illegal now. It is putting the minister above the subject. As we know, the minister is relying upon his commissioner of income tax for guidance in these matters, so much so that neither minister apparently is in a position to give the facts of the cases aimed at. That leaves the whole matter in a sea of doubt.

Certainly if this section is to be passed both here and in another place and become the law of the land, it is not unreasonable to ask the Department of National Revenue or the Department of Finance to table at some time during the session every exercise of this very special prerogative for which they are now asking. Parliament has the right to know what legislation is being passed, particularly when it is the crown which is taxing the subject rather than parliament which is levying the tax. I have asked the minister to give us some idea of the evils aimed at by this particular section, and that does not seem an unreasonable request to me. If the minister does not know the facts and principles in a few cases which the new section is to provide against, it is not likely that as a member of the treasury board he will have time to give judicial consideration to the claims of the subject. The whole idea that the treasury board be made a judicial body to sift the facts and give decisions in these cases seems to me to be a figment of the imagination. The whole thing will depend upon the officials of the department who will advise the minister, and the minister, in turn, holding the confidence of the treasury board will once again rule in these matters. Otherwise it is a physical impossibility for the treasury board to deal with these cases.
Why is the government seeking to have this blanket power given to the administration rather than to have taxes levied by parliament as is the constitutional right of a free parliament? It is because they have found that they cannot catch a few cases. As, however, I suggested the other day, parliament is sitting for at least six months in the year, and if there is a particularly bad case at hand parliament can always legislate retroactively if it meets the conscience of the legislators. But in order to satisfy the convenience of the taxing officials the government is willing to hamstring business. Business is not being consulted on this matter, and what the repercussions will be is not known. Every piece of legislation that is brought down through the Minister of Finance in regard to the method of revenue collection is concerned with departmental expediency, making it easier for the department, with little or no consideration being had for the individual. Certainly I had never heard of the individual being asked bow' it will affect him or how it will affect business generally. Every time there is a sale of a business the question of taxation is extremely important. As I mentioned the other night, no longer must the transaction satisfy a reasonable business purpose ; but if the government can point out that the main purpose, - according to their own

Income War Tax
view, is to avoid taxation, not to evade taxation, but merely to comply with the law with a resultant saving in taxes, then the department may levy the tax according to its own ideas.
There is no doubt that at the present time, with the government collecting 40 per cent of all corporate profits and sharing in none of the losses, there is not the zeal to pay taxes that there might be. In fact, the government is in a better position than if it owned all industry, because it collects 40 per cent of the profits and shares in none of the losses. They seem to overlook the fact that capitalism, like medicine, buries its mistakes and that only those ventures which are successful are extant. It was put to me in this way by one gentleman, and I would ask hon. members to bear this analogy in mind. It is lawful for a man to walk down one side of a street in order not to have bricks fali on his head. But the effect of this law, when he does walk down the lawful side of the street, is to declare that in so doing he did an unlawful thing. Such arbitrary and ex post jacto powers take away from the individual his essential freedom of action, his liberty. For example, under such legislation a strike which may be legal may be declared illegal by some government-appointed committee. It is not set forth anywhere what is wrong and what is right. It is entirely in the minds of the ministers and those who advise them.
May I point out in this regard that the minister had some unkind words to say the other day about tax avoidance. Tax avoidance is merely complying with the law so that one will not have to pay more taxes than one has to. I have not heard of anybody who is desirous of paying more taxes than he has to. That is perfectly natural. But they are all willing, so far as I know, to pay their just taxes. So that there is no tax evasion; there is a lawful avoidance of tax wherever possible.
The minister said the other day, reading from an English tax journal, that tax avoidance was something different from what it used to be; that it was almost as bad as evasion; that it was perhaps not exactly treason, but something to be considered most unpatriotic and unsocial. May I say again that if he is going to leave the determination of law to the minds of individuals rather than have it on the statute books, where the people of this country can see for themselves what the law of the land is, we shall have a very peculiar situation. This matter of ministerial allowances for motorcars has been up a number of times, and I do not intend to speak upon that subject on the eve of a victory loan; but may I tell the minister
that when he talks about the action of some people in avoiding - taxes as very nearly treasonable, other people may have strange ideas about ministerial motorcar allowances.
The fundamental law of this land should not rest in the hands of an individual. If this law goes through, if I may employ a simile, there is no longer freedom of action to walk down either side of the street. It is no longer sound common sense to walk down the clear side and thus avoid falling bricks. You are to be treated as though it is your duty to walk where the bricks are falling. The minister is virtually saying that a man is not justified ini not acting so as to render himself liable to taxation but should have walked so 'as to render himself liable to taxation. Such a situation, the minister must realize, is contrary to human nature, even human nature in war time, when people are willing to contribute in accordance with what is the Law of the land' but not according to what some person may have in his mind for the time being. No matter how able that official, or even the minister for the time being, may be, we know that both officials and ministers are subject to change. So that, wheither it be overtime work or the saving of capital, it has always been found that, since human nature is what it is, progress depends to a large extent upon selfinterest; and that if people are to proceed and do their business they must know what the law of the land is, and the law must not rest in the mind of the minister or even of some official; it must be clearly set forth in black and white on the statute books of this country.

When the minister during previous discussions of this matter made the statement that it was just about impossible for the department to keep up with devices imagined' and concocted by people who are engaged to help corporations to avoid paying income tax, he stated from his official position an opinion which is held quite widely, particularly among working people throughout the country. I recall also that, when questioned on this matter the other night, he stated that we were talking not about small potatoes but about big money. I concur in the remarks which were made by many others, including the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar, that it is to be hoped that in days to come we shall find ways to do this slightly different from the way that is being used just now. But I am quite satisfied that the country will be with the minister in his endeavour, particularly now, where large sums are involved, and when
Income War Tax

people are making sacrifices for the war and feel that this kind of thing should not take place. I am satisfied that the people will support him in what he is doing in this section.

This enables me to bring up the question which I raised last night. It seems to me that now is the time when consideration should be given to the type of case to which I then referred. I have reference, of course, to the case of the illegitimate child in the home of the mother who is unmarried and looking after her child and is subject to income tax as a single person. In the case which I had brought to my attention and to which I referred last evening, the mother I understand is on a small salary and is maintaining her child, and she is unable to make any deduction because neither can she

adopt her own child nor under the law is the child recognized as her dependent or her child. It seems to me that this is the time when something might be done to meet such cases. Since the matter was argued last evening I simply wish to say that in my opinion, when a child is born under such circumstances, and the mother can care for that child, it is better that the child should remain with the mother than be taken away or abandoned or placed in some charitable institution. The mother should not be placed in the position where she finds it difficult not only to maintain herself but to feed, clothe and educate the child properly. It seems to me that the ruling of the Department of Justice is wrong and that we are perpetuating the survival of a wrong principle that came to us through the ages, inflicting punishment upon the child for the misbehaviour of the parents. In my opinion 'we should wipe out this blot. After all, many of our aristrocratic families in the British commonwealth trace their descent back to the mistresses of kings. If we inquire into their pedigrees we find that illegitimacy in their case was regarded as a mark of blue blood. We have inherited one standard for one class of people and another for another class. As the hon. member for Vancouver East said last night, if you look at this problem in the proper light there are no illegitimate children, but there are illegitimate parents.
I plead with the minister that if the interpretation of the department is according to accepted law, some slight change might be made in the wording of this section in order to allow the unmarried mother to retain her child and raise it in a respectable manner in her own home, and receive the exemption that any mother should receive in order to bring up her child in her own home.

I thoroughly agree with
the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar as to the need for providing that an unmarried mother be allowed income tax exemption for the purpose of supporting an illegitimate child. I do not, however, agree with him that the Department of Justice is wrong in the decision tendered to the Department of National Revenue. Under statute law "child" has to be interpreted on a great many occasions. There are occasions when it is wise and' proper that the word be confined to its legitimate sense. In this particular case the remedy lies, I think, in the definition of "dependent" in the act itself. While the minister may hesitate to consent offhand to a change, the importance and extent of which he may not be able to determine quickly, I certainly wish to support the plea of the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar that the min-

Income War Tax
ister give consideration to the definition of that word "dependent" in this act, and that if at all possible provision be made for such a mother to have an exemption on behalf of that child.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do not recall this particular request with regard to illegitimate children ever coming up in the house or in committee of the whole before. It has been presented very forcibly and in a way to appeal to our sympathies, and1 it may have considerable merit. But I point out that it would be a very serious and far-reaching departure from the principles which have been followed from the beginning of this act in 1917.
The principles have been fairly clear. So far as children are cbncerned, we recognize children who are children of the taxpayer in the legal sense, or children by adoption, but all through the years illegitimate children have never been recognized. The plea has been to recognize foster children of various kinds, two or three years ago it was British guest children; but we have never seen our way to change the fundamental principles of the act.
When taxation gets high I can understand that the question becomes much more acute, but I could not undertake to do such a far-reaching thing as this on short notice. All I can promise is that it will be given consideration. There is of course the possibility of action under the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act, but offhand it would appear to me that one should hesitate very much before beginning to use that procedure.
However, I would be prepared to give consideration even to that in some of these extreme cases. It might very well be that if anything were to be done along this line there should be conditions. Insistence on adoption might be desirable. It might be that the surroundings were not such that income tax exemption is the proper thing from the social point of view; I do not know about that. It means a very considerable credit on tax bills, and as I say it would be completely at variance with the principles of our taxation system as they have existed ever since 1917.

Probably the reason why this question has not been raised before is that none of us knew of the existence of the problem. It is because a letter came to my desk yesterday morning from a point in Ontario that it was brought to my notice. I had no idea that woman maintaining her child, whether legitimate or illegitimate, was not entitled to the deduction. Not being a lawyer, I did not know the legal definition of "child".
I accept the correction made by' the hon. member for Swift Current. Perhaps I was inaccurate in stating that the ruling of the Department of Justice is wrong. Legally and according to precedent they are probably right, but I can find no moral justification for the ruling.
There should be a remedy.

I do not know how the minister can find the remedy, but I hope he will give the matter earnest consideration. I realize that what he has said is from his point of view perfectly sound regarding the implications of an amendment.

It was brought up two
years ago.	.

I hope this phase will be duly considered and a remedy found.
I agree with the minister that if we are to allow income tax exemption on account of such children, it may be desirable that we should see the home is a proper home, and so on. But we do not do that in the case of persons who are married, where home conditions are sometimes poorer than in a home of the kind I described this afternoon, which is good. The point is that girls who have illegitimate children and wish to care for them cannot claim deductions from their incomes and cannot get the consent of the children's aid societies to adoption, because the societies maintain that the children are the girls' own children and that, therefore, there is no force in going through the form of adoption. Then they are in difficulties. I feel certain that sympathetic consideration will be given to our pleas.

speechtext: The only thing the hon. gentleman brought up was the question of guest children. He may have placed a question on the order paper in regard to foster children, but he was most zealous in trying to get exemption for these British guest children, and he did not bring up the general question of foster children. That is my clear recollection, and I should remember that, because I argued with him about it enough to know his position.

There is no doubt about the zealousness with which I presented the case in regard to British guest children. I think I touched upon the others also, perhaps more inferentially than directly. Nevertheless I strongly support the point of view expressed by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar. Last night I asked the minister whether he would not agree that every child in Canada who is not kept at an institution should be the subject of income tax exemption. There may be some factors which those of us on the . outside, who do not have all these questions coming before us, have not considered. If there are such factors I think the minister should tell us about them, in order that we may disabuse our minds of any wrong thinking on this matter. Otherwise we would be encouraged to hold our view that every child in Canada should be the subject of income tax exemption.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Why stop at children? Why not include all worthy recipients of private benefaction, all worthy recipients of support? If the hon. gentleman received the letters that we receive from people who say, "You should allow me an exemption because I am supporting a friend or relative who is ill in my home," he would realize what this means. We must have some rules and some limits to this thing. The general rule is that contributions to charitable institutions and organizations may be deducted from income for tax purposes up to a certain amount, I think, ten per cent of the income. The general rule in regard to dependents, however, is that if a person undertakes something which it is not his obligation to undertake, though .it may be very desirable to undertake, in the way of a private charitable activity, he does so on his own responsibility and the government makes no concession to him for it. Perhaps the government should step in; perhaps it should reward him for his good-heartedness, but this government does not and I do not know of a government that does. That is something he does himself. He does that out of his tax-paid income, not out of his non-tax-paid income. I may not be 100 per cent correct in this, but the almost universal rule is that the deductions are made for the support of dependents whom the taxpayer is under a legal obligation to support, not somebody whom he chooses to support or somebody whom he charitably supports. That is the basis of the act; that is why it applies to children, either legitimate or adopted, and not to illegitimate children; that is why it applies to a wife and not a common-law wife. Perhaps sometimes it should properly apply to a common-law wife, if we are to take a broad view of these matters. I do not know what is to be said about that; certainly we recognize it in the pension legislation. I am just pointing out that we are opening up a field here of tremendous extent, and the hon. gentleman cannot stop at children. He would have to include any child, a niece, a nephew, a stranger or anyone a taxpayer might take in and feed. He cannot stop there; he has to take in everybody whom he helps in this way, and it is not consistent with the principles on which our system is built.

Perhaps the minister will give consideration, as he has suggested, to the point raised, and see if it is at all possible to do anything under the present taxation regulations or if perhaps some amendment would be required. I think it is a point that the minister might well take into consideration.

Mr. O'NEILL: This afternoon the hon. member for Cape Breton South was speaking about taxation on payment for overtime. In British Columbia we have a great number of shipyard workers, longshoremen and railway workers. Many of these railway workers who are on spare boards may work one week and earn $50 or $60, while the next week they may earn nothing at all. It seems to me that some plan could be worked out under which an average rate would be applied to these men working on spare boards, because during the weeks they earn S60 or $65 they are taxed at the rate at which they would be taxed if they earned that much for fifty-two weeks in the year, which they do not. Some consideration should be given in these cases. I do not know just how it could be done, but if you tax a man at a rate much higher than you should, a great deal of money will have to be returned.
I should like to say a word with regard to the refundable portion of the tax. I do not know whether the practice is the same in the Canadian National, but in the Canadian Pacific, when a man receives his cheque at the end of a work period, on the end of that cheque there is a stub. On the face of the stub is shown the amount of money he has made, and the deductions therefrom. Then there is an indication of what those deductions are for. It seems to me that in respect of this returnable portion of the tax some plan of that kind might be devised by employers. It is a good idea. When an employer gives his employee a cheque, with stub attached, the employee can keep the stub. Then at the end of the year he knows exactly what has been taken from him by way of taxation, and he can find out from the Department of National Revenue how much is returnable. Otherwise he has no record at all.
The vast majority of men to-day who have wage deductions through taxation do not believe they will ever get back that returnable portion. They believe that that is just so much hooey, and they have no way of knowing how much has been taken away from them. If a practice of this kind were adopted, they would at least have a record of the money taken from them. This is something which
the Minister of National Revenue might consider carefully, because I know it works satisfactorily in respect of the employees of the Canadian Pacific. It saves the railway a lot of trouble, and it saves the superintendent a great amount of correspondence when answering questions as to the reasons for deductions.
